chapters.title: Welcome to the Associate Foundations Certification
chapters.html:
About this certification

Anthropic's Claude Certified Associate – Foundations validates that knowledge workers and business users can work productively with Claude. It covers the 4Ds AI Fluency Framework (Description, Delegation, Diligence, Discernment), Claude workspace features (Artifacts, Code Execution, Projects, Skills, Memory, Connectors), prompting, iterative refinement, model selection, evaluation, and responsible AI practices.

Exam format

The exam contains 60 questions mixing three formats:

  • Single choice: select the best answer from four options.
  • Select two: choose exactly two correct answers from five options.
  • Sequence ordering: arrange steps in the correct order.

All questions and options are verbatim from the real exam bank. Each question tests a practical scenario you will face when using Claude at work.

Who is Maya?

Maya Chen is a business operations analyst at Brightline Services, a mid-sized professional services firm. Her team handles client onboarding, quarterly reporting, policy documentation, and process optimization. Maya has never used AI tools professionally before, but her manager asked her to explore how Claude could speed up recurring documentation tasks.

Over the next 30 days, Maya goes from her first Claude chat to becoming her team's AI-fluent lead. Each chapter of this guide follows her journey: the problems she faced, the concepts she learned, how she applied them at work, and what the exam tests about those topics.

How to use this guide

  1. Read each chapter and press Play on animations (nothing autoplays).
  2. Answer knowledge-check questions before opening the answers.
  3. Take the mock exam in chapter 14 in one sitting.
  4. Use chapter 13 (exam playbook) for final review before your real exam.

Storyline map: Maya's 30-day journey

  • Week 1 (ch. 2-5): Maya learns the 4Ds, writes her first prompts, creates her first Artifact, and masters iteration.
  • Week 2 (ch. 6-8): Maya sets up a Project for her team's quarterly reports, discovers Code Execution for exact calculations, and connects Google Drive.
  • Week 3 (ch. 9-10): Maya learns which model to use when, decomposes a complex workflow, and designs human review gates.
  • Week 4 (ch. 11-12): Maya audits her workflows for PII risks, builds evaluation checklists, and learns to catch hallucinations.
  • Exam prep: Maya reviews the playbook (ch. 13) and takes the mock exam (ch. 14).
Accuracy: All exam questions are real. Concepts align with official Claude documentation (claude.ai, November 2026). The 4Ds AI Fluency Framework is widely recognized for business AI adoption. Maya's scenarios are illustrative composites of common workplace situations.

scene.title: What does Claude actually do?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Day 1 – "What does Claude actually do?"

Maya's manager handed her a stack of quarterly client reports and said, "See if Claude can help." Maya had no idea where to start. She opened Claude and typed, "Help me with reports." Claude replied with generic advice about report structure. Maya realized she needed a framework for how to work with AI, not just what to type.

She found Anthropic's AI Fluency Framework, built around four competencies knowledge workers need: Description, Delegation, Diligence, and Discernment. Each one answered a question she had faced that morning.

takeaways: Description: state what Claude reliably produces, its limitations, and which human review stays in place; it underpins the other three Ds.
Delegation hinges on two criteria: does the task need uniquely human judgment or empathy, and is it reversible / how costly is an error?
Diligence is a sustained habit: apply AI policy and quality checks to every output, every day, not just at onboarding or under audit.
Discernment: verify claims against primary sources, not secondary AI summaries, and pinpoint suspected hallucinations before escalating.

chapters.title: The AI Fluency Framework: The 4Ds
chapters.html:
2.1 Description: Explain what Claude can and cannot do

What is it?

Description is the competency of accurately explaining Claude's capabilities, limitations, and the human oversight that remains in place, calibrated to your audience's familiarity with AI.

Why is it needed?

Stakeholders (managers, clients, teammates) need realistic expectations. Overpromising creates disappointment; underestimating it wastes opportunities. Transparent description builds trust.

How does it work?

When explaining a Claude use case, state three things:

  1. What Claude reliably produces for this task
  2. Known limitations or failure modes
  3. Which human review or decision-making stays in place

Tailor the detail to whether your audience has used AI before.

Real-world analogy

Like a job reference: you describe what the candidate is great at, where they need support, and what supervision looks like — not a sales pitch, not a pessimistic warning, but a balanced picture.

Practical example

Maya told her manager: "Claude can draft our quarterly summary from the data we upload, but I'll need to verify every number against the source file and check that the narrative matches our client's terminology. It won't replace my review; it gives me a faster first draft."

When to use it

Use Description when proposing a new use case, reporting results to a sponsor, or onboarding a teammate. It is the foundation of the other three Ds.

Examination relevance

Exam questions on Description test whether you can frame a use case transparently — naming capabilities and limitations together, and avoiding both overconfidence ("Claude does it all") and excessive caution ("never trust AI"). Description competency and Executive framing are pure Description scenarios.

2.2 Delegation: Decide what tasks to give Claude vs. keep human

What is it?

Delegation is the competency of deciding which workflow steps are appropriate to delegate to Claude and which must remain with human staff, based on task characteristics and consequences.

Why is it needed?

Not every task should be automated. Some require human creativity, empathy, or accountability that Claude cannot provide. Others carry risks (e.g., legal liability, PII exposure) that make delegation unsafe without controls.

How does it work?

Two criteria guide Delegation decisions:

  1. Does the task need uniquely human judgment, empathy, or creativity? If yes, keep it human or use Claude only as a draft
  2. Is the task reversible, and what is the consequence of an error?

High-consequence irreversible tasks (e.g., legal commitments, clinical decisions, promotion rulings) require human ownership.

Real-world analogy

Like assigning work to an intern: you delegate research and drafts, but you keep final sign-off, client-facing commitments, and judgment calls that could affect someone's livelihood.

Practical example

Maya delegated "draft the metrics summary from the uploaded spreadsheet" to Claude, but kept "decide whether the client renewal is at risk" as her own judgment call, informed by Claude's summary.

When to use it

Use Delegation when designing a new workflow, auditing an existing one, or evaluating whether a proposed use case crosses a line.

Examination relevance

Delegation criteria is the canonical Delegation question: it asks which two criteria inform whether to delegate. Use case safety and Appropriate delegation test use-case appropriateness (is this safe to delegate?). The exam often pairs a safe use case (e.g., "draft training summary from approved docs") with an unsafe one ("make promotion decisions").

2.3 Diligence: Apply policies and quality checks consistently

What is it?

Diligence is the competency of applying organizational AI policies, quality standards, and verification steps consistently as a sustained professional habit, not just during audits or high-visibility tasks.

Why is it needed?

One-off compliance during onboarding is not enough. Policies protect the organization and individuals (e.g., PII rules, bias checks). Diligence means checking every output, not only when someone is watching.

How does it work?

Treat AI governance like expense-report rules: you follow them because they are policy, not because you feel like it that day. Identify gaps between actual usage and policy, and close them. Build checklists for recurring tasks.

Real-world analogy

Like hand-washing in healthcare: not just when a supervisor is present, but every single time, because the risk (infection) does not pause when no one is looking.

Practical example

Maya built a checklist: before sending any Claude output externally, she verifies no PII leaked, the facts match the source, and the tone matches Brightline's voice guide. She uses it on every client report, even low-stakes ones.

When to use it

Diligence applies to every workflow, every output, every day. It is the "how consistently do you actually do this" competency.

Examination relevance

Diligence in governance is the pure Diligence question: it contrasts one-time onboarding vs. sustained habit. Policy boundaries tests whether you respect policy boundaries (the "do not enter investigation data" rule) even when workarounds exist.

2.4 Discernment: Validate outputs and catch errors

What is it?

Discernment is the competency of critically evaluating Claude outputs for factual accuracy, hallucinations, unsupported claims, and misalignment with your criteria before relying on or sharing them.

Why is it needed?

Claude is a language model: it predicts plausible text, not truth. It can hallucinate sources, invent statistics, or confidently state falsehoods. Discernment prevents those errors from reaching clients or decision-makers.

How does it work?

For every output:

  1. Verify facts against authoritative sources (not other AI summaries)
  2. Check that claims are supported by the material you provided
  3. Compare the output to your task criteria (does it answer what you asked?)
  4. Flag ambiguous or suspiciously confident assertions for deeper review

Real-world analogy

Like fact-checking a draft from a very confident but occasionally wrong colleague: you trust the structure and prose, but you independently verify every claim before it goes into the final report.

Practical example

Maya asked Claude to summarize competitor pricing. Claude cited "three major competitors at $X-Y per seat." Maya checked: one competitor was real, two were hallucinated. She regenerated the prompt with "use only the uploaded competitor sheet; if a competitor is not listed, say so."

When to use it

Apply Discernment to every output before you rely on it, share it, or act on it. It is especially critical for external-facing content, financial data, and anything cited as fact.

Examination relevance

Fact-checking discipline, Primary source verification, and Hallucination triage are Discernment questions: they test whether you know to verify a claim against a primary source (not accept secondary repetition), locate original studies, and pinpoint suspected hallucinations before escalating.

Exam relevance: The 4Ds structure repeats across the exam. When you see "preparing a stakeholder communication" → Description. "Deciding which steps to delegate" → Delegation. "Applying policy consistently" → Diligence. "Validating a striking claim" → Discernment. Recognizing the D being tested is half the battle.

scene.title: Why is my procedure buried in chat scrollback?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Day 3 – "Why is my procedure buried in chat scrollback?"

Maya drafted a 10-step client onboarding procedure with Claude. She copied it into an email, but halfway through writing the email she realized a step was wrong. She scrolled back through 30 chat turns to find the procedure again. Her manager asked for an updated version two days later — Maya had no idea which chat it was in.

Her colleague showed her Artifacts: Claude can render the procedure as a standalone document in a dedicated panel, separate from the chat. The team can open it, edit it, save it, and come back to it later. No more hunting through scrollback.

takeaways: An Artifact is standalone work (document, code, chart, diagram) rendered in a dedicated side panel, separate from the chat transcript.
Artifacts persist across sessions, can be edited in place, versioned, and shared via a stable link with view, comment or edit permissions.
Decision rule: if the team will come back to edit, reference or share it, make an Artifact; a one-off answer or quick lookup stays in chat.
Artifacts and Projects both solve 'don't repeat yourself': Artifacts hold reusable deliverables, Projects centralize reference material.

chapters.title: Artifacts: Standalone documents you can save and share
chapters.html:
3.1 What Artifacts are and when to use them

What is it?

An Artifact is a standalone piece of work (document, code, chart, diagram) that Claude renders in a dedicated side panel, separate from the chat transcript. Artifacts persist across sessions, can be edited in place, versioned, and shared via a stable link.

Why is it needed?

Chat responses scroll away and get buried. Artifacts give your work a permanent home. Use them when the output is something the team will reference, update, or iterate on across multiple review cycles — not one-off answers.

How does it work?

Ask Claude to produce the content as an Artifact. Claude decides whether the request fits (substantial, reusable content) and renders it in the side panel. You can edit the Artifact directly, save versions, and share the link with teammates who can view, comment, or edit depending on permissions.

Real-world analogy

Chat is like a conversation transcript. An Artifact is like the whiteboard sketch you save as a photo so everyone can reference it later.

Practical example

Maya asked: "Create an Artifact with our 10-step client onboarding procedure." Claude rendered it as a document in the side panel. Two days later, Maya opened the same Artifact, asked Claude to add a step, and shared the updated link with her manager.

When to use it

Use Artifacts for: procedures, templates, reports, code, charts, project plans — anything the team will reference across multiple sessions. Do NOT use Artifacts for quick one-off answers ("What is our PTO policy?") — those stay in chat.

Examination relevance

Artifact use case is the canonical Artifact question: it contrasts generating a procedure in chat (bad: gets lost) vs. as an Artifact (good: stable reference). The exam tests whether you recognize that Artifacts are for reusable, team-facing work, not ephemeral answers.

3.2 Artifacts vs. chat responses

What is it?

The key distinction: chat responses are conversational turns that answer a question or explain something. Artifacts are deliverable work products the team will save, iterate, and reference.

Why is it needed?

Choosing wrong wastes time. Putting a procedure in chat means you lose it; rendering a one-sentence answer as an Artifact is overkill.

How does it work?

Ask: "Will the team come back to this later to edit, reference, or share it?" If yes → Artifact. If no (one-time answer, quick clarification) → chat response.

Real-world analogy

A chat response is like a Slack DM. An Artifact is like a Google Doc you share with the team.

Practical example

Chat: "What does our remote-work policy say?" — Claude answers in chat. Artifact: "Draft a remote-work FAQ the HR team can publish" — Claude creates an Artifact.

Examination relevance

The exam pairs use cases where Artifacts fit (team procedure, recurring report template) against ones where chat is fine (quick policy lookup). Always ask: is this a deliverable someone will reference later?

ScenarioOutput typeWhy
Draft a weekly status template the team will reuseArtifactReusable deliverable; team iterates on it
"What is the PTO accrual rate?"Chat responseOne-off factual answer; no iteration
Create a 5-section project proposal for stakeholder reviewArtifactMulti-section doc; reviewers will edit/comment
"Explain what Code Execution does"Chat responseExplanation, not a work product
Exam relevance: Workflow improvement also touches Artifacts indirectly: "extracting standard reference material into a Project" (A) is correct because it centralizes reusable content. Artifacts and Projects both solve the "don't repeat yourself" problem.

scene.title: Why does the same prompt give me different results?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 1 – "Why does the same prompt give me different results?"

Maya typed "Summarize this" and uploaded a 20-page client contract. Claude gave a 3-sentence overview. She tried again with the same prompt — this time Claude gave a 2-page bullet list. A third run produced a table. Same input, same prompt, wildly different outputs.

Her manager explained: "You told Claude what to summarize, but not who it is for, why, or what format you need. So Claude guessed differently each time." Maya learned that a well-structured prompt has four elements: role, context, task, and format.

takeaways: A well-structured prompt has four elements: role, context (audience, goal, constraints), task (the deliverable) and format.
Non-determinism is expected, not a bug: cut variance with explicit prompts, output examples, and Projects/custom instructions.
Match format to the use case: table for comparisons, bullets for scannable summaries, numbered steps for procedures, prose for narrative.
If outputs are inconsistent or incomplete, suspect under-specification first; time-pressed executives need bottom-line-up-front.

flow.title: Prompt structure: four elements, one consistent answer

chapters.title: Prompting fundamentals: Task, context, format, role
chapters.html:
4.1 The four elements of a well-structured prompt

What is it?

A prompt that reliably produces the output you need includes:

  1. Role — who Claude is acting as
  2. Context — audience, goal, constraints
  3. Task — the specific deliverable
  4. Format — structure, length, style

Why is it needed?

Without these, Claude fills in the blanks with its own assumptions — and those change run to run because the model is non-deterministic. Explicit prompts reduce variance.

How does it work?

Template: "You are a [role]. [Context: audience, goal]. [Task: specific deliverable]. [Format: structure, length, tone]." Not every prompt needs all four, but recurring workflows should specify them to get consistent results.

Real-world analogy

Like a work order: you tell the contractor what to build, why, who will use it, and how it should look. Leave one out and you get a surprise.

Practical example

Before: "Summarize this contract."
After: "You are a contract analyst. Summarize this 20-page service agreement for our CFO, who needs to understand payment terms, renewal dates, and liability caps before the board meeting. Provide a 1-page summary with three sections: Payment Terms, Renewal & Termination, and Liability. Use bullet points."

Examination relevance

Prompt elements asks which two elements belong in a business prompt: (A) clear task statement and (B) relevant context (audience, goal). Prompt quality is similar for a prompt-quality checklist. Task completeness tests task specificity: when Claude skips a question, strengthen the task statement to enumerate all required questions.

4.2 Why prompts produce different outputs across runs

What is it?

Claude is a non-deterministic model: even with identical input, it can produce different outputs because it samples from a probability distribution over possible next tokens.

Why is it needed?

This is not a bug. It reflects the creative flexibility of language models. But it means under-specified prompts drift unpredictably.

How does it work?

To reduce variance:

  1. Make the prompt more explicit (specify format, required sections, tone)
  2. Provide examples of the desired output
  3. Use Projects/custom instructions to lock in recurring rules

Real-world analogy

Like asking five designers to "make it look good" — you get five different aesthetics. Give them a brand guide and required layout, and the outputs converge.

Practical example

Prompt under-specification: a weekly status prompt produces inconsistent tone/structure across runs. Root cause: the prompt under-specifies audience, tone, format, and required sections (B). Fix: spell out the target audience, list the mandatory sections, and state the tone ("professional, no contractions").

Examination relevance

The exam tests whether you know non-determinism is expected (A in Prompt under-specification is a trap: "accept the variation") vs. addressable by better prompting (B is correct: specify what is missing).

4.3 When to specify format explicitly

What is it?

Some tasks communicate best in a specific format: tables for comparisons, bullet lists for scannable summaries, prose for narratives. Specifying format in the prompt ensures Claude matches your need.

Why is it needed?

Claude chooses a format if you do not. Sometimes it guesses right; often it does not. Explicit format requests eliminate that guess.

How does it work?

Common formats: Table (compare metrics across teams/regions), Bulleted list (action items, findings), Numbered steps (procedures), Narrative prose (executive summary, explanation). State the format in the task: "Provide a table with one row per region and columns for revenue, growth, and variance."

Practical example

Output format selection: comparing weekly performance across five regional teams. Answer: a structured table with one record per row and one metric per column, sorted by region (C). Why? Tables make cross-team comparison immediate; prose summaries bury the comparison.

Examination relevance

Format questions test whether you match the deliverable to the use case. Comparison → table. Scannable summary → bullets. Narrative explanation → prose. Audience adaptation tests audience adaptation: time-constrained executives need BLUF (bottom-line-up-front), not chronological build-up.

Exam relevance: Prompt quality is tested in Prompt under-specification, Prompt quality, Task completeness, Prompt elements, Hallucination root cause, Terminology alignment. The pattern: under-specification causes drift/omissions/hallucinations. The fix: make the task, format, and constraints explicit. On exam day, if a prompt is producing inconsistent or incomplete outputs, always suspect under-specification first.

scene.title: This output is close but not quite right
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 2 – "This output is close but not quite right"

Maya asked Claude to draft a quarterly client summary. The first version was too long, used the wrong tone, and missed a key metric. She tried rewording the prompt eight times. Versions 6, 7, and 8 all had the same flaw: the executive summary buried the bottom line three paragraphs down.

Her colleague asked, "Did you tell Claude what was wrong and what you needed instead?" Maya had been guessing at prompt changes without diagnosing the specific problem. She learned the diagnose-revise-verify loop: pinpoint the flaw, fix it with a targeted follow-up, then check whether it worked.

takeaways: Refinement runs in order: diagnose the specific weakness, revise with a targeted fix, verify it worked, then decide what's next.
Three consecutive near-identical outputs with the same flaw means diminishing returns: stop prompting, edit by hand or change approach.
Productive feedback responses: map each reviewer comment to a specific change, and ask clarifying questions when feedback is ambiguous.
Disciplined iteration fixes only what reviewers flagged: leave accepted parts alone, don't rewrite from scratch or add unrequested changes.

flow.title: Iterative refinement: diagnose, revise, verify, decide

chapters.title: Iterative refinement: The diagnose-revise-verify loop
chapters.html:
5.1 The four-step refinement loop

What is it?

Effective iteration follows four steps in order:

  1. Diagnose: identify the specific weakness in the current output against your criteria
  2. Revise: craft a follow-up prompt or edit that addresses that weakness
  3. Verify: check whether the new output fixed the problem without breaking something else
  4. Decide: accept, iterate again, or try a different approach

Why is it needed?

Random prompt tweaks waste time and often make things worse. Disciplined iteration converges faster and avoids regressions (fixing one thing, breaking another).

How does it work?

Before you change the prompt, write down exactly what is wrong: "The executive summary does not lead with the headline result." Then craft a targeted fix: "Move the headline financial result to the first sentence of the executive summary." Generate, check, repeat if needed.

Real-world analogy

Like debugging code: you don't randomly change lines hoping it works. You identify the failing test, understand why it fails, fix that specific line, and re-run the test.

Practical example

Maya diagnosed: "The summary is 3 pages; I need 1 page. The tone uses contractions; our style guide forbids them. The churn metric is missing." She revised: "Shorten to 1 page. Use formal tone with no contractions. Add the churn metric in the metrics table." The next output nailed it.

Examination relevance

Refinement sequence asks the correct order of refinement steps. Answer: Identify specific weaknesses (D) is first, before modifying the prompt (A), submitting it (C), or comparing the result (B). The sequence is always diagnose → revise → verify → decide.

5.2 When iteration hits diminishing returns

What is it?

After several iterations, if the last 2-3 outputs are nearly identical and still have the same minor flaw, you have hit diminishing returns: more prompting will not fix it.

Why is it needed?

Some problems cannot be solved by better prompting — they need direct human editing, a different tool (e.g., Code Execution for math), or a change in approach (e.g., decompose the task).

How does it work?

Track your iteration count and the changes across runs. If 3 consecutive outputs are nearly identical, stop prompting. Options:

  1. Manually edit the flaw
  2. Switch tools (Artifact → direct edit, or add Code Execution)
  3. Decompose the task into smaller prompts

Real-world analogy

Like tuning a guitar: small adjustments converge to "close enough." Once you are within a few cents and further tweaks do nothing, you are done — use the guitar or get a tuner.

Practical example

Diminishing returns: eight iterations, last three nearly identical with the same minor flaw. Answer: Iteration has reached diminishing returns; next step is human review or a different approach (C). The exam contrasts this with "keep trying" (A, wrong) and "accept as-is" (D, wrong — the flaw still needs fixing).

Examination relevance

Disciplined iteration reinforces this: when reviewers accept a prototype except for two specific concerns, address those two directly and leave accepted parts unchanged (A). Do not rewrite from scratch (D) or add unrequested changes (C) — disciplined iteration fixes only what is broken.

5.3 Productive feedback responses

What is it?

When teammates review a Claude draft and give feedback, two responses are productive:

  1. mapping each piece of feedback to the specific change made in the next draft
  2. asking clarifying questions when feedback is ambiguous before acting on it

Why is it needed?

Vague iteration (e.g., "I incorporated your feedback") leaves reviewers guessing what changed. Clarifying ambiguous feedback prevents wasted work.

How does it work?

For each reviewer comment, either: show the specific edit it drove, or ask "Do you mean X or Y?" before revising. Track accepted vs. deferred feedback so reviewers know what landed.

Practical example

Feedback discipline: which two feedback responses are productive? (A) Mapping each feedback item to the specific change and (C) asking clarifying questions on ambiguous feedback. The exam contrasts these with traps: deferring all feedback (B), trusting Claude output blindly (D), or applying contradictory edits simultaneously (E).

Examination relevance

Feedback questions test discipline: act on clear feedback with traceable changes; clarify ambiguous feedback before acting; do not defer everything, trust blindly, or apply conflicting changes.

Exam relevance: Iteration is tested in Feedback discipline, Refinement sequence, Diminishing returns, Disciplined iteration, Terminology alignment. The meta-pattern: diagnose specifically, revise targeted, verify the fix, and stop when prompting hits diminishing returns. The exam penalizes random tweaking, ignoring feedback, and rewriting from scratch when small edits suffice.

scene.title: Why am I pasting the same instructions into every chat?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 2 – "Why am I pasting the same instructions into every chat?"

Maya was drafting quarterly client summaries for eight clients. Every chat started with the same 300-word block: "You are a client-success analyst. Our tone is professional with no contractions. Always include these five sections: Executive Summary, Metrics, Key Wins, Risks, Next Steps. Here is our terminology guide…"

Her manager said, "Set up a Project. Put those instructions in once, upload the terminology guide, and every chat in the Project gets them automatically. No more copy-paste." Maya created the "Quarterly Client Summaries" Project. Her prompts shrank from 400 words to 50, and every output followed the rules without her repeating them.

takeaways: A Project bundles custom instructions, uploaded knowledge and Skills; every chat in it inherits them. Use for recurring work, not one-offs.
When authoring custom instructions, define the Project's purpose and boundaries first, then draft, validate and refine them.
Fix weak Project output by being explicit: name the role, tone (no contractions), minimum length, required sections and attached policy.
Use a Skill by adding it, uploading knowledge and writing instructions that reference both. Review configs periodically as policies change.

flow.title: Projects: one brief, every chat inherits it

chapters.title: Projects: Centralize instructions and knowledge for recurring workflows
chapters.html:
6.1 What Projects are and when to use them

What is it?

A Claude Project is a shared workspace that bundles custom instructions (recurring rules that apply to every chat in the Project), knowledge (uploaded docs Claude can reference), and Skills (specialized workflows). Every chat in the Project inherits these settings.

Why is it needed?

Recurring workflows waste time re-explaining the same rules. Projects eliminate repetition and ensure consistency: everyone on the team gets the same instructions, the same reference docs, the same tone.

How does it work?

Create a Project for workflows that repeat: monthly reports, client onboarding, policy Q&A. Write custom instructions that define Claude's role, required format, tone, and mandatory sections. Upload reference docs (style guides, templates, policies). Add relevant Skills if available.

Real-world analogy

Like a shared folder with a README: the folder holds the reference files, the README holds the rules everyone follows when working in that folder.

Practical example

Maya's "Quarterly Client Summaries" Project custom instructions: "You are a client-success analyst at Brightline Services. Produce quarterly summaries for enterprise clients. Tone: professional, empathetic, no contractions. Structure: Executive Summary (headline result first), Metrics (table), Key Wins (bullets), Risks (bullets), Next Steps. Use terminology from the uploaded glossary. Cite client data files by name."

When to use it

Use Projects for recurring workflows where the task structure, tone, reference docs, or required format stay constant across runs. Do NOT use Projects for one-off exploratory chats.

Examination relevance

Workflow improvement: "extracting standard reference material into a Project" (A) improves a recurring workflow because it avoids repeating that material in every prompt. Project instruction authoring tests the order of steps when writing custom instructions: define the Project's purpose and boundaries (D) before drafting, validating, or refining the instructions.

6.2 Custom instructions: The rules that apply to every chat

What is it?

Custom instructions are the recurring rules you write once at the Project level. They define Claude's role, required output format, tone, mandatory sections, and any constraints (e.g., "never reveal account numbers").

Why is it needed?

They eliminate the need to repeat the same preamble in every chat. They also enforce consistency: every teammate's chat follows the same rules.

How does it work?

Write instructions as if briefing a new teammate: "Your role is X. When you produce Y, always include Z. Our tone is A, not B. Here are the rules: …" Be explicit about required sections, forbidden actions, and where to find reference material.

Practical example

Project instruction tuning: a Project for customer incident follow-ups produces drafts that are too brief, offer unauthorized credits, and use prohibited contractions. Fix: "Specify brand voice attributes (empathetic, formal, no contractions), set a minimum length, and instruct Claude to recommend a goodwill credit only when the attached eligibility policy permits one" (C).

Examination relevance

Project instruction tuning and Project instruction design test whether you know how to write effective custom instructions. The pattern: be explicit (name the role, format, tone, required sections), reference attached knowledge ("check the attached policy"), and state constraints ("minimum length," "no contractions").

6.3 Skills: Pre-built workflows you can add to a Project

What is it?

A Skill is a specialized workflow (e.g., course design, slide generation, research synthesis) that Anthropic or your organization provides. Skills integrate into Projects to guide Claude on complex recurring tasks.

Why is it needed?

Skills codify best practices for specific workflows, so you do not have to invent the instructions from scratch.

How does it work?

When setting up a Project, check if a relevant Skill exists. Add the Skill, upload supporting knowledge docs, and write custom instructions that reference both the Skill and the knowledge.

Practical example

Skill integration: to leverage a Skill in a course-design Project, add the Skill, upload supporting knowledge sources, and write custom instructions that reference both (D). The exam contrasts this with contradictory instructions (A), disabling the Skill (B), or writing unrelated instructions (C).

Examination relevance

Skill questions are rare but test integration: add the Skill, coordinate it with knowledge and custom instructions; do not contradict or disable it.

6.4 When to update Project configurations

What is it?

Even well-configured Projects drift over time as organizational policies, terminology, and reference docs evolve. Configurations should be reviewed and updated periodically.

Why is it needed?

A Project locked in 2025 rules will produce outdated outputs in 2026, even if quality has not visibly degraded yet.

How does it work?

Schedule periodic reviews (quarterly or when policies change). Check: Are the custom instructions still accurate? Are the uploaded docs current? Has terminology changed?

Practical example

Configuration maintenance: a colleague never updates their Project because "if it works once, it works forever." Feedback: Configurations should be reviewed periodically because policies, terminology, and source docs change over time (B). Configuration drift: outputs cite outdated terminology/sources → the configuration needs updating (C).

Examination relevance

The exam tests whether you know Projects require maintenance, not one-time setup. Watch for "outdated terminology" or "policy changed" as signals to update.

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

scene.title: Why is this total wrong by $3,000?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 2 – "Why is this total wrong by $3,000?"

Maya uploaded a 50-row expense spreadsheet and asked Claude to sum column D. Claude replied: "The total is approximately $47,300." Maya checked manually: the real total was $44,287. She asked again — Claude said $46,950. "Approximately" was not acceptable for a finance report.

Her manager explained: "Claude is a language model. It predicts plausible text, including plausible-looking numbers. For exact arithmetic, use Code Execution — Claude writes Python code, runs it in a sandbox, and gives you the verified result." Maya enabled Code Execution, uploaded the file again, and got the exact total: $44,287.

takeaways: Language models predict plausible text, they do not compute; for exact arithmetic, statistics or data transforms, use Code Execution.
Code Execution writes Python, runs it in a sandbox and returns code plus output; signal words: exact, compute, calculate, plot, visualize.
Always verify: read the code (right file, right column, right filter) and spot-check the result against the source data before sharing.
The exam contrasts Code Execution with plain chat (unreliable for math), Artifacts (not for calculation) and Research (not for computation).

flow.title: Code Execution: exact numbers, not predictions

chapters.title: Code Execution: When you need exact calculations, not predictions
chapters.html:
7.1 What Code Execution is and when to use it

What is it?

Code Execution is a Claude feature that runs Python code in a sandboxed environment to perform deterministic calculations, data analysis, file processing, and chart generation. The code and its output are returned to you for verification.

Why is it needed?

Language models predict text; they do not compute. For tasks requiring exact arithmetic, statistics, or data transformations, relying on text prediction produces errors. Code Execution delegates the math to Python, which computes exactly.

How does it work?

When you upload a data file (spreadsheet, CSV, dataset) and ask for calculations or a chart, Claude writes Python code, executes it in a sandbox, and shows you the code + output. You verify the code makes sense and the result is correct before using it.

Real-world analogy

Like the difference between asking someone to estimate a sum in their head (unreliable) vs. handing them a calculator (exact).

Practical example

Code Execution use case: a finance manager needs exact summary totals across a multi-tab spreadsheet. Answer: Use Code Execution, which runs code to calculate exact totals the manager can verify (D). The exam contrasts this with plain chat (A, unreliable for arithmetic), Artifacts (B, not for calculation), and Research (C, not for computation).

Examination relevance

Code Execution questions test whether you know when to use it: exact calculations, summary statistics, data transformations, chart generation. The signal words are "exact," "compute," "calculate," "summary statistics," "plot," "visualize."

7.2 Verifying Code Execution outputs

What is it?

Code Execution shows you the Python code it ran and the output. You must verify the code is correct (does it actually do what you asked?) and check the result against the source data before relying on it.

Why is it needed?

Claude can write buggy code or misunderstand your request. Blindly trusting the output without verification defeats the purpose.

How does it work?

Read the code: Does it load the right file? Does it sum the right column? Does it filter correctly? Then spot-check the output: pick a few rows from the source file and confirm the calculation matches.

Practical example

Code Execution + verification: compute summary statistics and a chart from an uploaded dataset. Answer: Use Code Execution to calculate and generate the chart, then verify the computed results against the source data before sharing (D). The exam penalizes estimating from a preview (B) or describing what the chart would show (C) instead of generating it.

Examination relevance

Verification is mandatory: the correct answers in Code Execution use case and Code Execution + verification both include "verify the output" as part of the workflow. Never accept Code Execution results without checking them.

Exam relevance: Code Execution is tested in Code Execution use case and Code Execution + verification. The pattern: if the task requires exact arithmetic, statistics, or visualization from uploaded data, use Code Execution. Always verify the code and output before sharing. The exam contrasts this with plain chat (unreliable for math) and Artifacts (not for computation).

Knowledge check

scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 3 – "Why doesn't Claude remember what I told it yesterday?"

Maya spent Monday explaining Brightline's client tiers to Claude in detail. Tuesday she started a new chat and asked about tier-2 renewal policies — Claude had no idea what tier 2 meant. Every chat started from scratch.

Her colleague said, "Enable Memory. Claude will remember preferences and context across chats." Maya enabled it, told Claude once about the tier structure, and from then on every chat knew the tiers without her re-explaining them. She also connected Google Drive so Claude could pull client files directly instead of her uploading them manually every time.

takeaways: Memory keeps recurring facts (your role, org structure, terminology) across chats; keep task-specific details like quarterly numbers out.
Memory imports from other platforms are experimental and may not bring everything over; add missing details manually in Settings.
Connector indexes refresh periodically, so a document revised hours ago may not show yet; the cause is index lag, not permissions.
When a long chat loses coherence, summarize the current state and continue with a focused follow-up; do not discard it all or swap models.

flow.title: Memory: Claude remembers the tiers across chats

chapters.title: Memory and Connectors: Persistent context and workspace integration
chapters.html:
8.1 Memory: Persistent context across chats

What is it?

Memory is a Claude feature that retains information across chat sessions. You can tell Claude facts, preferences, or context once, and it will remember them in future chats without you repeating.

Why is it needed?

Repeating the same context in every chat wastes time. Memory eliminates that repetition for recurring facts (your role, your organization's structure, terminology).

How does it work?

Enable Memory in Settings. Tell Claude information you want it to remember: "Remember: Brightline has three client tiers. Tier 1 = enterprise ($50k+ ARR), Tier 2 = mid-market ($10k-50k), Tier 3 = SMB (under $10k)." Claude stores this and references it in later chats. You can view, edit, or delete stored memories in Settings.

Real-world analogy

Like onboarding a new teammate: you explain the org structure once; they remember it for future conversations.

Practical example

Maya told Claude her role, Brightline's tier definitions, and their quarterly reporting cadence. From then on, every chat started with that context already loaded.

When to use it

Use Memory for recurring facts (org structure, terminology, your role, constraints) that apply across many chats. Do NOT use it for task-specific details (this quarter's numbers, this client's contract).

Examination relevance

Memory imports tests Memory imports: Memory imports from other platforms are experimental and may not incorporate all content automatically (B). You can manually add missing details via Settings.

8.2 Connectors: Integrate Google Drive, Slack, and other tools

What is it?

Connectors let Claude access content from external workspaces (Google Drive, Slack, etc.) so it can reference files, messages, or data without you manually uploading them every time.

Why is it needed?

Manual uploads are slow and error-prone. Connectors automate the fetch and keep Claude's context aligned with your live workspace.

How does it work?

Connect the integration in Settings (e.g., Google Drive). Claude can then search your Drive, read documents, and reference them in responses. Permissions respect your access: Claude sees only what you can see.

Real-world analogy

Like giving a contractor access to your shared Dropbox instead of emailing them files one by one.

Practical example

Maya connected Google Drive. She asked, "Summarize the Workflow improvement client summary for Acme Corp." Claude found the file in her Drive, read it, and summarized it — no manual upload.

Examination relevance

Connector index refresh is the connector gotcha: connector indexes refresh periodically, so a document revised three hours ago may not be reflected yet (D). The exam contrasts this with permissions (A), Claude selecting an older version (B), or caching (C) — the real cause is index lag.

8.3 Context windows: How much Claude can consider at once

What is it?

A context window is the bounded amount of text (measured in tokens) that Claude can consider in a single request, including the system instructions, conversation history, attached files, and your current input.

Why is it needed?

Once the conversation grows beyond the window, earlier turns are dropped or compressed. Understanding this helps you design workflows that stay within limits.

How does it work?

Long conversations eventually exceed the window. When that happens:

  1. Summarize the current state and start a focused follow-up
  2. Use Projects to offload recurring instructions
  3. Decompose large tasks into smaller prompts
  4. Use Memory for recurring facts instead of repeating them in every turn

Real-world analogy

Like a desk: you can only fit so many papers on it at once. When it is full, you either summarize what is there and clear space, or move some papers to a filing cabinet (Memory/Projects).

Practical example

Context recovery: a long conversation starts losing coherence. Recovery: Summarize the current state and continue with a focused follow-up prompt (B). The exam contrasts this with replacing the model (A, wrong), discarding everything (C, wasteful), or escalating (D, overkill). Context window definition defines a context window correctly as (A).

Examination relevance

Context questions test whether you know:

  1. It is bounded
  2. Old turns drop when it fills
  3. The fix is summarize + focus, not discard everything or switch vendors

Knowledge check

scene.title: Why is this costing so much?
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 3 – "Why is this costing so much?"

Maya used Claude Opus (the most capable model) for everything: drafting emails, summarizing one-page memos, answering quick policy questions. Her manager saw the usage report: "You are burning through our rate limit on tasks a lighter model could handle. Use Opus for complex analysis; use Sonnet or Haiku for routine summaries."

Maya learned the model trade-off: more capable models are slower, consume more of the rate limit, and cost more. Lighter models are faster and cheaper but less capable on complex reasoning. The right model depends on the task.

takeaways: Haiku: lightweight, fast, cheapest. Sonnet: balanced mid-tier. Opus: most capable but slower, with the highest rate-limit use and cost.
Decision rule: Haiku for simple, well-defined tasks; Sonnet for most production workflows; Opus for one-off problems needing deep reasoning.
The trade-off the exam tests: more capable models generally run slower and consume more rate limit, so match the model to task complexity.
Recurring workflows: set the quality/latency/volume bar, test a candidate on samples, keep the lightest that passes, retest on new models.

flow.title: Model selection: match the model to the task

chapters.title: Model selection: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus trade-offs
chapters.html:
9.1 The model family: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus

What is it?

Claude offers three model tiers: Haiku (lightweight, fast, cheapest), Sonnet (balanced, mid-tier), and Opus (most capable, slower, highest rate-limit consumption and cost).

Why is it needed?

Not every task needs the most capable model. Using Opus for simple tasks wastes cost and rate limit; using Haiku for complex reasoning produces weak results. Matching the model to the task optimizes quality, speed, and cost.

How does it work?

Decision rule: Use Haiku for simple, well-defined tasks (summarize a short doc, extract structured data, quick Q&A). Use Sonnet for most production workflows (drafting reports, multi-step reasoning). Use Opus for one-off complex problems requiring deep reasoning, creativity, or nuanced judgment.

Real-world analogy

Like choosing a vehicle: a bike (Haiku) is fast and cheap for short trips; a sedan (Sonnet) handles daily commutes; a truck (Opus) is for heavy loads or rough terrain.

Practical example

Maya switched to Sonnet for her weekly client summaries (routine multi-step task) and reserved Opus for analyzing a complex contract dispute (one-off deep reasoning). Haiku handled quick policy lookups.

Examination relevance

Model selection: a one-off complex problem requiring extended multi-step financial reasoning → Opus, positioned as most capable for advanced reasoning (C). Model trade-off: more capable models generally run slower and consume more rate limit (D). The exam tests whether you know the trade-off exists and can match model to task complexity.

9.2 Aligning model selection to a recurring workflow

What is it?

For recurring workflows, model selection follows a sequence: define quality/latency/volume requirements, choose a candidate, test it on representative samples, select the lightest model that meets the bar, and retest when new models launch.

Why is it needed?

Starting with the heaviest model wastes cost; starting with the lightest risks poor quality. Testing with real samples finds the right fit.

How does it work?

Steps:

  1. Define the quality bar ("summaries must include all five sections"), latency tolerance ("under 10 seconds"), and expected volume
  2. Choose a candidate model based on that profile
  3. Run representative samples and measure quality, latency, rate-limit consumption
  4. Select the lightest model that consistently meets the bar
  5. Retest when new models become available

Practical example

Model selection sequence: aligning model selection to a recurring workflow. Correct order: 3 (define bar/tolerance/volume), 4 (choose candidate), 1 (run sample and measure), 2 (select lightest that meets bar), 5 (retest when new models launch) (A).

Examination relevance

Sequence questions test whether you define requirements first, test second, and select the lightest passing model (not the heaviest or most expensive).

Knowledge check

scene.title: This request is too big for one prompt
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 3 – "This request is too big for one prompt"

Maya's manager asked her to "Redesign the new-hire onboarding process." Maya typed that into Claude. Claude gave a vague 3-paragraph overview. She tried again with more detail — the output was slightly better but still shallow.

Her colleague said, "That request has three distinct deliverables: a process map, supporting training materials, and a measurement plan. Break it into three focused prompts; each one will be stronger than trying to do all three at once." Maya decomposed the task. Each prompt produced a specific, well-structured deliverable. She combined them into a final proposal.

takeaways: Decompose when a request needs multiple distinct deliverables (map + materials + plan); one complex deliverable still gets a single prompt.
Over-decomposition reads fragmented and choppy; the fix is to consolidate related steps into fewer cohesive sections, not add headings.
A reliable human-in-the-loop hand-off documents both what Claude must produce and the exact criteria the reviewer checks before approval.
Improve recurring workflows structurally: move repeated reference material into a Project and add a quality gate before downstream use.

flow.title: Task decomposition: three focused prompts beat one

chapters.title: Task decomposition and workflow design
chapters.html:
10.1 When to decompose a task

What is it?

Task decomposition is breaking a broad request into multiple focused sub-prompts, each producing one specific deliverable, instead of asking Claude to do everything in one go.

Why is it needed?

A single prompt trying to do too much produces shallow, generic outputs. Focused prompts let Claude apply its full reasoning to each piece.

How does it work?

Ask: Does this request require multiple distinct outputs (e.g., a map + materials + a plan)? If yes, decompose. Write one prompt per deliverable. Combine the outputs at the end.

Real-world analogy

Like a work breakdown structure: you do not ask a contractor to "build the house" in one step. You break it into foundation, framing, electrical, plumbing — each one done well.

Practical example

Decomposition signal: "redesign new-hire onboarding" requires multiple distinct outputs: a process map, supporting materials, and a measurement plan (D). That signals decomposition will help. The exam contrasts this with single structured documents (A), familiar formats (B, C) — those do not need decomposition.

Examination relevance

Decomposition questions test whether you recognize multiple distinct deliverables as the signal. One deliverable, even if complex → single prompt. Multiple deliverables → decompose.

10.2 Over-decomposition: When you break it too small

What is it?

Breaking a task into too many tiny steps fragments naturally connected ideas and makes the output choppy and hard to follow.

Why is it needed?

Over-decomposition is as bad as under-decomposition. Fifteen one-sentence steps is worse than three cohesive sections.

How does it work?

Balance: decompose enough to give Claude focus, but not so much that related ideas are torn apart. If the output feels fragmented, consolidate related steps into fewer cohesive sections.

Practical example

Over-decomposition: a procedure decomposed into fifteen narrow steps looks fragmented. Fix: Consolidate related steps into fewer cohesive sections that group naturally connected ideas (A). The exam contrasts this with merging steps by sequence (B, wrong) or just adding headings (D, cosmetic fix).

Examination relevance

Watch for "fragmented," "choppy," "related ideas split apart" as signals of over-decomposition. The fix is always consolidate, not add more structure on top.

10.3 Workflow hand-offs: Defining what Claude produces and what the human reviews

What is it?

A reliable human-in-the-loop hand-off documents both what Claude is expected to produce (scope, format, required elements) and the specific verification criteria the human reviewer must check before approving.

Why is it needed?

Vague hand-offs ("review this for quality") lead to inconsistent reviews and missed issues. Explicit criteria ensure every reviewer checks the same things.

How does it work?

Write two checklists:

  1. Claude's deliverable spec (sections, format, tone, length)
  2. Human reviewer's checklist (verify facts against source, check tone matches brand guide, confirm all required sections present, etc.)

Document both in the workflow.

Real-world analogy

Like a QA checklist on a production line: the spec says what the product should be; the QA checklist says what the inspector verifies.

Practical example

Hand-off design: designing a hand-off between Claude drafting and a human reviewer. Answer: Define explicit criteria for what Claude produces and what the human reviewer must check before approval, documented in the workflow (B). The exam contrasts this with leaving reviewer checks unspecified (C) or letting each reviewer decide (D).

Examination relevance

Hand-off questions test whether you know both sides must be explicit: what AI does + what human checks. One-sided definitions (only Claude's spec or only reviewer criteria) are incomplete.

10.4 Improving recurring workflows

What is it?

Two changes meaningfully improve recurring workflows:

  1. Centralizing standard reference material into a Project (avoiding repetition)
  2. Adding a quality check that gates outputs before downstream use

Why is it needed?

Repetition wastes time; missing quality gates let bad outputs through.

How does it work?

Audit the workflow: What do people paste into every prompt? → Move it to a Project. Where do outputs go unchecked into the next step? → Add a verification gate.

Practical example

Workflow improvement: which two changes improve a recurring workflow? (A) Extracting standard reference material into a Project and (D) adding a quality check before outputs enter downstream processes. The exam contrasts these with cosmetic changes (section headings, workspace names) that do not reduce rework or catch errors.

Examination relevance

Workflow improvement questions test whether you recognize structural fixes (centralize repetition, gate quality) vs. cosmetic ones (rename things, reorganize headings).

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

scene.title: “Can I use this data with Claude?”
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 4 – "Can I use this data with Claude?"

Maya was drafting a summary from a spreadsheet of employee performance reviews. Halfway through, she realized: "Wait — this has salary figures, manager feedback, and accommodation notes. Is this safe to put into Claude?" She stopped, consulted the HR policy, and found the answer: No. Employee PII, compensation data, and medical notes must never enter AI tools without redaction.

Maya learned to classify data before prompting: identify sensitive fields, redact or anonymize them, then submit only the safe remainder. She also learned which use cases are appropriate (drafting training docs) vs. inappropriate (making promotion decisions).

takeaways: Data-handling sequence: classify sensitive fields, redact with placeholders, peer-review the redaction, then submit the safe remainder.
Keep final employment, legally binding and clinical decisions human-owned; drafting from approved docs and aggregated feedback is safe.
When policy prohibits entering data, escalate and refrain. Incognito is not an exemption and paraphrasing is not compliance.
Revise demographic generalizations into observed behaviors validated against real data; a disclaimer alone is not a fix.

flow.title: Data sensitivity: classify, redact, review, then submit

chapters.title: Responsible AI: Data sensitivity, bias, and use-case appropriateness
chapters.html:
11.1 Identifying sensitive data that requires redaction

What is it?

Sensitive data includes PII (names + government IDs, full payment-card numbers), confidential business data (unreleased financials, M&A plans), employee records (salary, performance notes, accommodation requests), and legal/medical information under privilege or HIPAA.

Why is it needed?

Even in Claude's standard service, entering sensitive data without authorization violates policy and creates risk. Some data must be redacted or excluded entirely.

How does it work?

Before submitting any document:

  1. Classify its contents (which fields are sensitive?)
  2. Redact sensitive fields and replace with placeholders (e.g., "[EMPLOYEE_ID]", "[SALARY]")
  3. Peer-review the redacted doc to confirm redaction is complete
  4. Submit the redacted version

Real-world analogy

Like preparing a deposition transcript: you black out privileged material before the other side sees it.

Practical example

Data classification: which data is appropriate in a routine prompt? (B) A redacted job description and (C) an anonymized policy summary. Wrong: named salary figures (A), accommodation notes (D), employee IDs (E). PII identification: customer government IDs + full card numbers tied to names (A) require redaction. Data handling sequence: the first step is classify and identify which fields are sensitive (A).

Examination relevance

Data-handling questions test the four-step sequence: classify, redact, peer-review, submit. Never skip classification. Named PII, salary, medical notes, and full card numbers always require redaction or exclusion.

11.2 Use cases that are inappropriate for Claude

What is it?

Some tasks should not be delegated to Claude, even with review:

  1. Making final decisions that materially affect someone's employment (promotions, terminations)
  2. Issuing legally binding commitments without attorney review
  3. Clinical or diagnostic decisions without clinician review
  4. Approving final external press releases without human sign-off

Why is it needed?

These tasks require human accountability, legal responsibility, or professional licensing that Claude cannot provide.

How does it work?

Decision rule: Can an error in this task harm someone (financially, legally, medically, reputationally) in a way that cannot be easily reversed? If yes, keep it human-owned or require strict human review before any action.

Real-world analogy

Like corporate signatory authority: certain decisions (sign a contract, approve a regulatory filing) can only be made by authorized humans, not delegated to an assistant.

Practical example

Use case safety: which use cases are acceptable? (A) Drafting internal training summary from approved docs and (B) synthesizing customer feedback themes under aggregation rules are safe. Wrong: determining promotions (E), issuing legal summaries without attorney review (C in some contexts), or clinical summaries without clinician oversight (D). Appropriate delegation is similar.

Examination relevance

Use-case questions contrast safe delegation (drafts, summaries from approved sources) with inappropriate delegation (final decisions affecting employment, legal/clinical practice). The signal words are "final," "binding," "promotion," "termination," "diagnostic."

11.3 Organizational policy boundaries: When to stop and escalate

What is it?

When an organizational policy explicitly prohibits entering certain data into AI tools (e.g., "no ongoing investigation data"), you must refrain and escalate for an approved alternative — even if workarounds (Incognito, paraphrasing) exist.

Why is it needed?

Workarounds do not override policy. Policy boundaries protect the organization and individuals; bypassing them creates liability.

How does it work?

If a task requires data that policy prohibits: stop, escalate to the policy owner (legal, HR, compliance), and wait for an approved workflow. Do not enter the data, do not use Incognito as an exemption, do not paraphrase to "get around" the rule.

Real-world analogy

Like an access control policy: if the door says "Authorized Personnel Only," you do not pick the lock or tailgate behind someone — you get authorization or stay out.

Practical example

Policy boundaries: HR policy prohibits entering ongoing investigation data into AI tools. Answer: Escalate to HR leadership and do not enter the data (C). Wrong: using Incognito (B), paraphrasing (D), or waiting until the investigation closes (A) — the policy applies now.

Examination relevance

Policy questions test whether you respect hard boundaries. Incognito is not an exemption. Paraphrasing is not compliance. When policy says no, the answer is escalate and refrain.

11.4 Bias and demographic generalizations

What is it?

Claude outputs can contain demographic generalizations (e.g., "this age group prefers X") that do not hold for individuals. Responsible use requires revising generalizations to focus on observed behaviors and validating against actual data.

Why is it needed?

Demographic generalizations risk stereotyping and systematic bias, even in internal documents.

How does it work?

When reviewing outputs: flag any statement that generalizes about a demographic group. Revise to describe observed behaviors (e.g., "customers in this segment clicked Y at rate Z") instead of group-level claims. Validate against actual customer data.

Practical example

Bias mitigation: a customer-segment description applies a demographic generalization unsupported by individual data. Fix: Revise to focus on observed behaviors and validate against actual customer data (D). Wrong: keeping it for internal use (A), adding a disclaimer (B), or removing the whole section (C). Ethical risks: highest ethical risks in HR workflows are (A) outputs disadvantaging protected groups and (E) decisions affecting employment without human accountability.

Examination relevance

Bias questions test whether you know to revise generalizations (not just disclaim them) and validate against data. The exam also tests whether you recognize systematic bias as a higher risk than typos or formatting inconsistencies.

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

chapters.teaser: A 300% growth stat with three sources turns out to be invented, and Maya learns to pinpoint, verify and escalate before it reaches the board.

scene.title: This growth stat looks too good to be true
scene.html:
Maya's story: Week 4 – "This growth stat looks too good to be true"

Maya asked Claude to research competitor growth rates. Claude replied: "Competitor A grew 300% last year (source: TechPulse, IndustryToday, MarketWatch)." Maya was drafting this into a board slide when she thought: "300% sounds high. Let me check the sources." She searched for the TechPulse article — it did not exist. IndustryToday mentioned Competitor A but said 30%, not 300%. MarketWatch never covered them.

Maya had caught a hallucination: Claude invented a plausible-sounding stat and fabricated sources to support it. She learned the fact-checking discipline: when a claim is striking or consequential, verify it against a primary source before relying on it.

takeaways: Define evaluation criteria and the acceptance threshold before scoring outputs; valid criteria are format adherence and factual accuracy.
Suspected hallucination: pinpoint the unsupported claim, verify it, and only if false regenerate with a stricter use-only-the-file prompt.
Secondary repetition is not verification; when sources conflict, locate the primary or authoritative source and use what it confirms.
Escalate high-impact outputs: external, unchanged, binding commitments to customers, board or regulators; internal drafts need none.
chapters.title: Evaluation and hallucination handling
chapters.html:
12.1 Defining evaluation criteria before scoring outputs

What is it?

Evaluation criteria are the specific, measurable standards an output must meet to be acceptable (e.g., "includes all five required sections," "facts match the source file," "tone is formal with no contractions"). Criteria must be defined before you score the output.

Why is it needed?

Without explicit criteria, "good enough" is subjective and inconsistent across reviewers. Defining criteria up front ensures every output is judged against the same bar.

How does it work?

For recurring workflows:

  1. Define what "acceptable" means (required sections, factual accuracy, tone, length)
  2. Specify the threshold (e.g., "at least 90% factual accuracy" or "all five sections present")
  3. Build a checklist
  4. Score every output against the checklist before approving it

Real-world analogy

Like a rubric for grading essays: you define the criteria (thesis, evidence, structure) before you read the first essay, not after.

Practical example

Evaluation criteria: valid criteria for a business brief include (A) alignment with requested format/length and (D) factual accuracy against supplied sources. Evaluation sequence: before scoring, you must (E) define evaluation criteria and (C) specify the threshold that separates acceptable from unacceptable.

Examination relevance

Evaluation questions test whether you know to define criteria first (before generating or scoring), and whether you can distinguish valid criteria (format adherence, factual accuracy) from invalid ones (word count vs. industry benchmarks).

12.2 Recognizing and handling hallucinations

What is it?

A hallucination is when Claude generates plausible-sounding but unsupported or false information: fabricated sources, invented statistics, confident assertions not backed by the material you provided.

Why is it needed?

Language models predict plausible text, not truth. They can confidently state falsehoods, especially when filling gaps in their knowledge.

How does it work?

When you suspect a hallucination:

  1. Pinpoint the specific claim that seems unsupported
  2. Verify it against an authoritative source (the document you provided, a primary study, official records)
  3. If it is false, regenerate with a stricter prompt: "Use only facts present in the uploaded file. If the file does not state X, say so."
  4. Document the pattern if it repeats

Real-world analogy

Like fact-checking a very confident but occasionally wrong source: you independently verify claims before accepting them as true.

Practical example

Hallucination triage: when a hallucination is suspected, the first step is pinpoint the specific claim that appears unsupported (C). Then verify it. Do not discard the whole output (D), notify users (B), or document it (A) before confirming it is actually false. Hallucination root cause: summaries include unsupported claims → root cause is prompt does not constrain Claude to use only supplied-source facts (A).

Examination relevance

Hallucination questions test the sequence: pinpoint → verify → regenerate with stricter constraints. Never accept striking claims without verification. The fix is always tighter prompting ("use only the uploaded file"), not hoping it goes away.

12.3 Fact-checking discipline: Verifying against primary sources

What is it?

When Claude cites a fact (especially a striking statistic, date, or claim), verify it against a primary or authoritative source, not secondary repetition. If secondary sources conflict, locate the primary source.

Why is it needed?

Secondary sources can repeat errors. Only the primary source (the original study, official record, company filing) confirms truth.

How does it work?

For every consequential claim: ask "What is the primary source?" Find it. Read the relevant section. Confirm the claim matches. If you cannot find the primary source, treat the claim as unverified and either exclude it or note it as unconfirmed.

Real-world analogy

Like verifying a rumor: you do not accept it because three people repeated it; you find the person who was there and ask them what actually happened.

Practical example

Fact-checking discipline: two secondary sources give conflicting dates. Fix: Locate a primary or authoritative source and use the date it confirms (D). Do not choose the newer one (A), the one with more detail (B), or average them (C). Primary source verification: trade-press articles repeat a growth figure without linking the study. Fix: Locate the original study and verify the figure in the primary source (D).

Examination relevance

Fact-checking questions test whether you know secondary repetition is not verification. Always trace back to the primary source. The exam penalizes accepting "three articles said it" as proof.

12.4 When to escalate outputs for review

What is it?

Escalation is required when an output has high impact (external-facing, binding commitments, financial/legal/reputational risk) and has not been reviewed by an appropriate human authority.

Why is it needed?

High-impact outputs that go out unchanged create liability if they contain errors.

How does it work?

Decision rule: Is this going to a customer, the board, a regulator, or the public? Does it commit the company to something (SLA, contract term, financial figure)? If yes, escalate for attorney/CFO/senior review before sending. Internal drafts for your own reference do not require escalation.

Real-world analogy

Like a signature authority policy: certain documents need VP sign-off before they leave the building.

Practical example

Escalation criteria: which output requires escalation? (C) An unchanged draft for a paying customer that includes a service-level commitment. Wrong: internal drafts for your own notes (A), casual internal status updates (B), or team meeting announcements (D) — none are external or binding.

Examination relevance

Escalation questions test whether you recognize high-impact external/binding outputs vs. low-impact internal drafts. The signals are "external," "unchanged," "paying customer," "commitment," "board," "regulator."

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

How to use this playbook

This chapter distills the 60-question exam bank into decision rules: "if you see X in the question, the answer pattern is Y." Read it once the night before your exam, then again 30 minutes before you start. These are the high-yield patterns that repeat across questions.

Output format selection

If the question says...The answer is...Why
"Team will reference this procedure across review cycles"ArtifactReusable deliverable; stable link (concepts: Artifact use case)
"Compare weekly performance across five regional teams"Structured table, one row per regionTables make comparison scannable (concepts: Output format selection)
"Compute exact summary totals from uploaded spreadsheet"Code ExecutionLanguage models predict; code computes exactly (concepts: Code Execution use case · Code Execution + verification)
"Quick policy question"Chat responseOne-off answer; no iteration needed

The 4Ds Framework

Question typeSignal wordsAnswer pattern
Description"Explain capabilities to stakeholders," "frame the use case"State what Claude produces AND limitations AND human oversight (concepts: Description competency · Executive framing)
Delegation"Decide which steps to delegate," "keep human vs. give Claude"Two criteria:
  1. Need for human judgment/empathy
  2. Reversibility + consequence (concepts: Delegation criteria)
Diligence"Apply policy," "consistent habit," "governance"Sustained habit, not one-time onboarding; close gaps over time (concepts: Diligence in governance)
Discernment"Validate a striking claim," "fact-check," "conflicting sources"Verify against primary/authoritative source; never accept secondary repetition (concepts: Fact-checking discipline · Primary source verification · Hallucination triage)

Prompting and iteration

SymptomRoot causeFix
Output inconsistent across runs (tone, structure, sections)Prompt under-specifies audience, tone, format, required sections (concepts: Prompt under-specification)Spell out all four: role, context, task, format
Claude skips one of three required questionsTask statement does not enumerate all questions (concepts: Task completeness)List all three explicitly and require an answer to each
Eight iterations, last three identical with same flawDiminishing returns (concepts: Diminishing returns)Stop prompting; apply human review or try different approach
Summary includes claims not in the sourcePrompt does not constrain to supplied facts (concepts: Hallucination root cause)Add: "Use only facts in the uploaded file; if not stated, say so"

Data sensitivity and use-case appropriateness

Data typeAction
Named employee salary, accommodation notes, full card numbers + namesRedact or exclude (concepts: Data classification · PII identification)
Redacted job description, anonymized policy summarySafe to include (concepts: Data classification)
Policy says "no investigation data in AI tools"Escalate and refrain; Incognito is not an exemption (concepts: Policy boundaries)
Use caseAppropriate?
Draft training summary from approved docsYes (concepts: Use case safety · Appropriate delegation)
Synthesize customer feedback themes under rulesYes (concepts: Use case safety · Appropriate delegation)
Determine promotion decisionsNo — requires human accountability (concepts: Use case safety)
Issue binding legal commitment without attorney reviewNo — requires professional sign-off

Projects and Memory

ScenarioAnswer
"Pasting same instructions into every chat"Move to Project custom instructions (concepts: Workflow improvement · Connector index refresh)
"Outputs cite outdated terminology/sources"Update Project configuration (concepts: Configuration drift · Configuration maintenance)
"Memory import missing some details"Imports are experimental; manually add via Settings (concepts: Memory imports)
"Google Drive connector shows old version (revised 3 hours ago)"Connector index has not refreshed yet (concepts: Connector index refresh)

Workflows and decomposition

PatternDecision
"Request requires process map + materials + measurement plan"Decompose into three focused prompts (concepts: Decomposition signal)
"15 narrow steps; output fragmented"Consolidate related steps into cohesive sections (concepts: Over-decomposition)
"Hand-off between Claude draft and human reviewer"Define what Claude produces AND what human checks, documented (concepts: Hand-off design)
"Improve recurring workflow"Centralize reference material into Project + add quality gate (concepts: Workflow improvement)

Model selection

TaskModel
One-off complex multi-step financial reasoningOpus (concepts: Model selection)
Routine weekly summaries, most production tasksSonnet
Quick policy lookups, simple extractionHaiku
More capable models......run slower, consume more rate limit (concepts: Model trade-off)

Hallucination and fact-checking

SituationAction
Suspect a hallucinated claimPinpoint the specific claim → verify against authoritative source (concepts: Hallucination triage)
Two secondary sources conflict on a dateLocate primary source; use the date it confirms (concepts: Fact-checking discipline)
Trade-press repeats a stat without linking studyFind the original study; verify in primary source (concepts: Primary source verification)
Summary includes unsupported claimsRegenerate with "use only supplied source" constraint (concepts: Hallucination root cause)

Evaluation

TaskSequence
Build evaluation checklist(E) Define criteria, (C) specify threshold, then score (concepts: Evaluation sequence)
Valid criteria for business brief(A) Format/length alignment, (D) factual accuracy vs. source (concepts: Evaluation criteria)
Report has all topics but one section under-scopedMeets topic-level presence but under-scoped; expand before delivery (concepts: Completeness vs. presence)

Exam traps to watch for

  • "Incognito lets you bypass policy" → FALSE. Incognito does not override organizational policy boundaries (concepts: Policy boundaries).
  • "Accept variation because models are non-deterministic" → NO. Variance is addressable by better prompting (concepts: Prompt under-specification).
  • "Three secondary sources said it, so it is true" → NO. Verify against the primary source (concepts: Fact-checking discipline · Primary source verification).
  • "Keep iterating forever" → NO. Stop at diminishing returns and apply human review (concepts: Diminishing returns).
  • "Rewrite from scratch after feedback" → NO. Address specific concerns; leave accepted parts unchanged (concepts: Disciplined iteration).
  • "Defer all feedback to a later cycle" → NO. Act on clear feedback now; clarify ambiguous feedback (concepts: Feedback discipline).

Final 24-hour checklist

  1. Re-read this playbook once.
  2. Take the mock exam (chapter 14) in one sitting.
  3. For each wrong answer: find the corresponding concept chapter and re-read that section.
  4. Sleep well. Arrive 10 minutes early. Read this playbook again in the waiting room.
The exam bank favors disciplined, transparent, and safe practices. When two answers seem close, ask: Which one is more explicit? Which one verifies facts? Which one respects policy boundaries? That is almost always the correct answer.
